name: Nmap
what: A network discovery and service inspection tool.
work: Checks reachable ports and probes service identity.
how: Start the local Red Team fixture, then run nmap -sT -p 8765 --reason 127.0.0.1. -sT tests a TCP connection; -p limits the port. An open result establishes reachability, not a vulnerability.

name: Burp Suite
what: An HTTP proxy and application testing workspace.
work: Inspects requests and responses and repeats controlled variations.
how: Use its integrated browser to visit the local marker URL. Find the request in Proxy history and send it to Repeater. Compare a known path with a nonexistent path, changing one input at a time.

name: OWASP ZAP
what: A web testing proxy with passive and active features.
work: Records browser traffic and highlights observations for review.
how: Use Manual Explore with the local fixture in Safe mode. Inspect History and response details. Automated Scan is a separate workflow that sends additional test traffic.

name: curl
what: A command-line data-transfer client.
work: Inspects HTTP status, headers and bodies.
how: With the local fixture running, use curl --max-time 5 -i http://127.0.0.1:8765/marker.txt. -i includes headers; --max-time bounds the request. Windows PowerShell users may need curl.exe to avoid an alias.

name: ffuf
what: A request-input comparison tool driven by a wordlist.
work: Substitutes candidate paths or inputs and compares responses.
how: Use the downloaded practice-paths.txt: ffuf -w practice-paths.txt -u http://127.0.0.1:8765/FUZZ -t 1 -rate 1 -maxtime 15 -mc all. Expect two known resources and one 404 on this fixture.

name: ProjectDiscovery httpx
what: An HTTP probing toolkit, distinct from the Python HTTPX library.
work: Summarizes endpoint status, content length and server observations.
how: Check httpx -h to confirm the binary. Use httpx -u http://127.0.0.1:8765/marker.txt -sc -cl -server -rl 1 -threads 1 against the running fixture. Server headers are evidence to validate, not proof of a vulnerability.

name: Metasploit Framework
what: A modular security assessment framework.
work: Provides modules with different purposes and operational effects.
how: In msfconsole select auxiliary/scanner/http/http_version, read info and show options, and set the local fixture host and port before run. Open the linked guide for the complete banner-check exercise.

name: Wireshark / TShark
what: Graphical and command-line packet analyzers.
work: Explain protocols and correlate observations with packet evidence.
how: Open an authorized lab.pcap and use the dns display filter. Or run tshark -r lab.pcap -Y "dns" -T fields -e frame.number -e dns.qry.name. No capture is supplied; encryption and capture position limit visibility.

name: BloodHound
what: An identity relationship and access-path analysis tool.
work: Helps investigate permission paths to sensitive resources.
how: Import an approved lab dataset, inspect a test-user path and read each edge prerequisite. Validate effective rights before claiming the path can be executed. Collection is a separate scoped activity.

name: Atomic Red Team
what: A library of small adversary-behavior tests.
work: Helps validate whether selected behavior produces expected defensive evidence.
how: In an existing reviewed lab with the module imported, use Invoke-AtomicTest T1082 -ShowDetails. Review commands, dependencies and cleanup before selecting execution; prerequisite operations can have side effects.

name: MITRE Caldera
what: An adversary-emulation orchestration platform.
work: Organizes abilities, agents, facts and operation plans.
how: In a disposable lab, review each ability and its privileges, dependencies and cleanup before any operation. Restrict the target group and define stop controls. The linked guide explains plan review; it does not install agents.

name: ATT&CK Navigator
what: A visualization tool for ATT&CK technique layers.
work: Communicates planned and tested behaviors using notes and a legend.
how: Create a layer, select supported behaviors, record evidence and scope, then export and reopen its JSON. A colored technique does not establish complete detection coverage.

name: Microsoft Sentinel
what: A cloud security monitoring and investigation platform.
work: Searches collected data and supports analytics and incident workflows.
how: Use an authorized KQL workspace and paste the downloaded sentinel-query.txt. The synthetic example should return trainee-a with three failures. Real data requires verified tables, schemas and connectors.

name: Splunk
what: A platform for searching and analyzing machine data.
work: Filters events, aggregates observations and supports alerts.
how: Paste splunk-query.txt into an authorized SPL search editor. Expect trainee-a with three failures from the synthetic data. Validate field extraction and time semantics before adapting it to an actual index.

name: Elastic / Kibana
what: A search and analysis stack with event exploration features.
work: Investigates indexed events and supports detection workflows.
how: In Discover select an authorized data view and bounded time range. For ECS events try event.category: authentication and event.outcome: failure. Kibana KQL differs from Microsoft Kusto KQL.

name: Wazuh
what: An endpoint monitoring and security analytics platform.
work: Decodes events and applies security rules.
how: On an existing lab manager run sudo /var/ossec/bin/wazuh-logtest and paste the synthetic JSON from the linked guide. Inspect decoded fields; a decoder match does not prove the whole collection pipeline works.

name: Sysmon
what: A configurable Windows system-monitoring service.
work: Records selected endpoint activity for investigation.
how: On an already configured lab host, inspect Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon/Operational in Event Viewer. Correlate process events with time and identity; available events depend on the configuration.

name: Zeek
what: A network traffic analysis framework.
work: Produces structured connection and protocol metadata.
how: Supply an authorized lab.pcap, create a fresh output folder and run zeek -r ../lab.pcap from it. Use zeek-cut for default TSV logs; which logs appear depends on traffic and policy.

name: Suricata
what: A network detection engine.
work: Inspects traffic and produces protocol events and rule-based alerts.
how: Validate the lab configuration with suricata -T -c /etc/suricata/suricata.yaml, using your actual configuration path. Then follow the offline-PCAP exercise. No alerts may mean no matching rule rather than safe traffic.

name: Sigma
what: A detection-rule format and tooling ecosystem.
work: Describes detection logic for conversion to supported analytics backends.
how: Read logsource, selection and condition. Inspect sigma --help and sigma plugin list, choose the correct backend and mapping pipeline, then validate generated queries with positive and negative fixtures.

name: CyberChef
what: A data-transformation workbench.
work: Decodes and transforms artifacts without executing their contents.
how: In an approved instance, paste U09DLVRFU1Q= and apply From Base64. Expect SOC-TEST. Save the recipe and explain the transformation; decoding alone does not establish malicious intent.

name: jq
what: A command-line JSON processor.
work: Selects fields, filters records and aggregates structured data.
how: In the extracted SOC folder run jq -s . auth-events.jsonl to view records as an array. The linked workbook shows the bounded failure-count aggregation and explains its stages.

name: YARA
what: A pattern-matching engine for file and memory content.
work: Applies explicit rules to identify patterns for investigation.
how: Use the inert malware-analysis fixtures and training-rule.yara.txt from the download. Compare positive and negative controls as described in the workbook. A rule match is not a malware verdict.

name: Shodan
what: A search service for indexed internet-facing service observations.
work: Helps investigate exposure using banners and timestamps.
how: Begin with your owned public asset inventory and a narrow search. Check freshness and ownership before treating a banner as current. Account capabilities vary; indexed searches differ from on-demand scans.

name: Gobuster
what: A discovery tool with web-path and other modes.
work: Compares candidate resources against a scoped service.
how: Read gobuster dir --help for your version, use a tiny training wordlist and an owned fixture, and establish a missing-path baseline. Validate responses before interpreting discoveries.

name: DirBuster
what: A graphical web content-discovery tool.
work: Requests candidate paths from a wordlist.
how: Use an owned training URL, a short wordlist and limited concurrency. Compare known and missing resources before a broader assessment. A response status alone is not a vulnerability.

name: Wappalyzer
what: A website technology identification tool.
work: Infers technologies from observable page and response features.
how: Inspect your training site using the approved extension or tool, then compare results with known implementation details. Fingerprints can be absent or misleading and do not prove vulnerability.

name: Subfinder
what: A subdomain discovery tool using passive sources.
work: Collects domain-name leads for inventory validation.
how: Review subfinder -h and provider requirements, then query an approved domain. Validate discovered names and ownership; results may be stale or point to shared infrastructure.

name: Nuclei
what: A template-based assessment engine.
work: Runs explicitly selected checks described by templates.
how: Read and validate the local training template from the advanced-web workbook, then use its bounded target and rate settings. Templates differ in effects and matches need confirmation.

name: Android Debug Bridge
what: The Android SDK interface for authorized debugging.
work: Inspects and manages an authorized emulator or test device.
how: Run adb devices -l, select your emulator serial and follow the linked package-inspection exercise. An unauthorized status means debugging trust has not been granted.

name: JADX
what: An Android bytecode decompiler and code viewer.
work: Helps inspect APK code and form static-analysis hypotheses.
how: Open your own training.apk with jadx-gui, review its manifest and trace a small code path. Decompiled output may differ from source; confirm behavior in a lab.

name: Apktool
what: An Android resource and bytecode representation tool.
work: Decodes APK contents for inspection.
how: Run apktool d training.apk -o decoded-training with your owned APK and a new output directory. Preserve the original; decoding alone does not establish a reachable weakness.

name: MobSF
what: A mobile application analysis framework.
work: Organizes automated observations about an app.
how: Analyze an owned training APK in an approved local deployment. Review each warning for code context, reachability and impact. Do not upload private builds to an unapproved service.

name: Frida
what: A runtime instrumentation toolkit.
work: Observes or changes behavior inside an instrumented process.
how: Start with a permitted debug training app and an unmodified baseline. Observe one harmless method and record inputs, outputs and instrumentation changes. Modified behavior is not automatically evidence of an original flaw.

name: Ghidra
what: A binary reverse-engineering framework.
work: Supports native-code disassembly and decompilation.
how: Import a benign owned library, confirm architecture and trace a known function. Decompiled code is approximate; correlate with source or controlled runtime evidence.

name: Volatility
what: A memory-forensics framework.
work: Extracts supported operating-system artifacts from memory images.
how: Use an authorized image and compatible symbols, determine its OS context and select a supported plugin. Preserve the original and acquisition notes; missing artifacts have interpretation limits.

name: TheHive
what: A security case-management platform.
work: Organizes evidence, investigation tasks and decisions.
how: Create a synthetic case in an approved lab, attach SOC fixture observations and assign follow-up tasks. Record confidence and alternatives; leave outbound response integrations disabled for practice.
